strengths: Well-motivated and challenging problem: reconstructing dynamic, emissive, high-frequency fire from only three views is a genuinely difficult setting that existing 4D Gaussian/NeRF methods do not address, and the paper is positioned honestly as a complete applied/systems pipeline rather than a new algorithmic primitive.

End-to-end system contributions are substantial and practical: a flow-initialized FreeTimeGS representation for fire, stereo+monocular depth fusion for the static background, explicit rolling-shutter handling, and a clever low-cost ESP32/LED Gray-code synchronization scheme that extracts microsecond-level timing from unsynchronized consumer cameras. This is a real enabler for affordable capture of fast phenomena.

A new real-world dataset (17 fire scenes, 3 synchronized 400 Hz GoPros, diverse fuels and backgrounds) with a stated commitment to release code and data; this is a valuable resource for a niche but relevant research area.

Reasonable experimental design: masked flame-region metrics (PSNRflame, SSIMflame), a depth-plausibility metric, and a broad ablation study (GlobalShutter, NoSync, RandFlow, JointOpt) reported per-scene in the supplement; the ablations support the key design choices, particularly the flow initialization and static/dynamic separation.
Clear limitations section that correctly identifies the main weaknesses (flow reliability under emissive variation, linear velocity model, static/dynamic separation assumption, sync precision).
weaknesses: The depth-based evaluation (RMSEdepth) is circular: the rendered depth is compared against the same monocular depth prior (DepthAnythingV2, linearly aligned) that is used for initialization and regularization of the method. A method strongly regularized toward this prior will trivially score better than baselines that were never given this prior, so the headline geometric-plausibility claim is only weakly supported. Ground-truth depth (e.g., a synthetic validation scene or a calibrated depth sensor) is missing.

Baseline comparison is narrow and arguably unfair in both directions: only two 4DGS baselines, tuned with author parameters from the DyNeRF flame_salmon scene (a different domain), random initialization, and with densification capped for Yang et al. Crucially, the direct foundation of the dynamic stage, FreeTimeGS [88], is not compared as a baseline (e.g., without the flow initialization), so the claimed benefit of the proposed representation versus simply running FreeTimeGS under the same preprocessing is not isolated. Tomographic flame reconstruction (Ihrke & Magnor) and physics-informed approaches are cited but not compared, even qualitatively, on any shared data.

Quantitative gains over the strongest baseline are modest in image space (PSNRflame +1.95 dB, SSIMflame +0.045 over 4DGS Yang) while 4DGS Yang actually wins full-frame LPIPS and PSNR; the main differentiator is the depth metric, whose circularity (see above) weakens the overall empirical case. No statistical significance testing is provided given the per-scene spread.

Evaluation is restricted to held-out frames on the same training trajectory; novel-view generalization is only shown qualitatively in a supplementary video. For a paper whose central claim is a 3D (not per-camera 2D) reconstruction of an under-constrained setup, quantitative novel-view or held-out-camera results would substantially strengthen the evidence.

Scope limitations that bound impact: only three-camera rigs with fixed geometry, 100-frame subsequences per scene, and no smoke-rich/large-scale scenes (acknowledged). The linear-velocity, per-Gaussian lifetime model is a fairly direct reuse of FreeTimeGS; the novelty is in assembly, initialization, and capture hardware rather than representation design.

strengths: Well-motivated and practically relevant problem: reconstructing fast, emissive, semi-transparent fire from only three commodity cameras is a genuinely hard and underexplored setting, and the pipeline (static/dynamic decomposition, stereo+monocular depth fusion for the background, flow-field initialization for fire Gaussians) is a coherent solution.

Significant systems and data contribution: a new real-world dataset of 17 fire sequences captured with a 400 Hz three-camera GoPro rig across diverse fuels (propane, wood, gasoline, cardboard, paper), with an LED-based Gray-code sub-frame synchronization scheme (~15 us precision) using rolling-shutter artifacts. This hardware contribution and dataset release are valuable to the community and appropriate for an Applied/Systems contribution type.

Thorough methodological care on capture-side issues that most 3DGS papers ignore, including explicit rolling-shutter modeling (Eq. 9) and sub-frame temporal alignment; the ablations (NoSync, JointOpt) show these matter for reconstruction quality and depth plausibility.

Reasonable ablation study (Tab. 2, Tabs. 7-10) demonstrating that flow initialization and static/dynamic separation are the key components (RandFlow and JointOpt degrade quality, JointOpt badly degrades depth), and per-scene results are provided in the supplement for transparency.

Code, a sample scene, and promise of full dataset release support reproducibility; limitations are honestly discussed (flow inaccuracies, linear velocity model, static/dynamic separation assumptions).
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core components are all existing methods assembled together — vanilla 3DGS, FreeTimeGS representation, MEMFOF optical flow, DepthAnythingV2, PatchMatchStereo, COLMAP. The main algorithmic additions (voxel-fused flow initialization with Tikhonov regularization, rolling-shutter delay approximation) are incremental and the rolling-shutter component is shown by the authors' own ablation (GlobalShutter) to have essentially no measurable effect.

The depth plausibility metric (RMSE_depth) is methodologically weak and partly circular: rendered depth is compared against linearly aligned DepthAnythingV2 predictions, yet the authors' own static-stage optimization uses exactly this monocular depth as a regularizer and initialization. Low RMSE_depth therefore partly reflects self-consistency with their own prior rather than independent evidence of geometric correctness; there is no ground-truth 3D evaluation at all.

Baseline comparison is potentially unfair and incomplete: only two 4DGS variants are compared, initialized randomly with hyperparameters tuned for the DyNeRF flame_salmon scene — an obvious mismatch the baselines are expected to fail under. Notably, FreeTimeGS itself (the representation the method builds on) is not evaluated as a baseline without the flow initialization, which would directly isolate the claimed contribution; MoSca, 4DGT, or a NeRF-based fire/smoke method are also absent.

Evaluation protocol has gaps: every-8th-frame held-out frames are still from the same three training viewpoints, so the reported metrics do not measure true novel-view synthesis quality, which is the central claim; quantitative evidence for generalization to genuinely new views exists only as qualitative supplementary video.

Several ablation gains are marginal (e.g., NoSync and GlobalShutter differ from the baseline by ~0.1-0.4 dB), weakening the practical importance of two of the four claimed contributions (hardware synchronization and rolling-shutter modeling) at the accuracy levels measured.

Presentation issues reduce polish: typos and grammatical errors ('Since observed a readout time', 'archives higher', 'offerfitting', 'moire patterns' rendering), inconsistent notation (RSME vs RMSE), and Table 1 reports the same LPIPS for Ours and GlobalShutter verbatim, raising questions of copy-paste.
The claim of 'microsecond-level synchronization' enabling the method is somewhat overstated given the NoSync ablation shows only a small quantitative drop.

strengths: Novel and practically relevant problem setting: 3D reconstruction of fire from only three cameras with consumer-grade hardware, which existing dynamic reconstruction methods and tomographic/physics-based fire approaches do not address.

Significant systems/engineering contribution: a low-cost, well-documented capture rig (3x GoPro at 400 Hz) with an ESP32-based LED Gray-code synchronization pattern that exploits rolling shutter to achieve ~15 us sub-frame synchronization - a clever and reusable hardware contribution.

A new real-world dataset of 17 diverse fire sequences (multiple fuels, backgrounds, and flame regimes) with per-scene documentation, promised public release alongside code - a valuable resource for the community.

Sensible methodological design: separating static/dynamic reconstruction, fusing stereo + aligned monocular depth for the under-constrained background, and initializing dynamic Gaussians from a multi-view fused 3D flow field solved with a clear least-squares formulation (Eqs. 5-8).

Reasonably thorough evaluation protocol: held-out frames, masked flame-region metrics, extensive per-scene results, and ablations covering each major component (sync, rolling shutter, flow init, joint vs. static pretraining).
Clear writing, well-structured pipeline description, and good qualitative figures including rendered depth comparisons; limitations are discussed candidly.
weaknesses: The geometric evaluation metric RMSE_depth compares rendered depth against a monocular depth prediction (DepthAnythingV2) after linear alignment. This is a weak, partially circular proxy: monocular depth is known to fail on transparent, emissive flames (the authors themselves note this), so using it both to regularize training and to claim that baselines 'spatially degenerate' weakens the central comparative claim. No independent geometric ground truth (e.g., surveyed scene geometry or a calibrated dense rig on a control scene) is provided.

Baseline coverage is thin: only two 4DGS variants, which were run with parameters tuned for an unrelated scene (flame salmon) and required memory-limit interventions. Notably, FreeTimeGS - the very representation the method builds on - is not evaluated as a baseline, nor are other sparse-view/monocular dynamic methods (Dynamic 3D Gaussians, MoSca, 4DGT), making it hard to isolate how much the flow initialization and static/dynamic split contribute versus the representation choice.

The quantitative advantage on flame regions over the strongest baseline (4DGS Yang) is modest (27.46 vs. 25.51 PSNR_flame), and that baseline wins on LPIPS, PSNR, and SSIM full-frame; 4DGS (Wu) is essentially a degenerate baseline in this setting, so the evidence for superiority is narrower than the framing suggests.

The rolling shutter modeling (Sec. 3.3) is presented as a contribution, but the ablation (GlobalShutter) shows no measurable quantitative benefit, and the authors ultimately approximate the model down to a constant offset t(p0); its practical value is therefore not demonstrated.

Quantitative evaluation uses only held-out frames along the training cameras; generalization to genuinely novel viewpoints is shown only qualitatively in supplementary video, which limits claims about 3D validity versus per-view overfitting - precisely the failure mode attributed to baselines.

Novelty is largely integrative: the core representation is FreeTimeGS with added flow-based initialization and a static/dynamic decomposition using standard components (3DGS, PatchMatchStereo, DepthAnythingV2, MEMFOF). Individual algorithmic novelty beyond the flow-fusion formulation and sync hardware is limited.

Minor presentation issues: typos ('Since observed a readout time', 'archives', 'offerfitting', 'evaluate all scenes' vs 'evaluated all'), Eq. 5's back-projection notation is under-specified, and the LED synchronization pattern contaminates the captured images (requiring masking), which is a practical drawback not fully weighed in the discussion.

strengths: The paper identifies and clearly articulates a genuine failure case of existing dynamic Gaussian Splatting methods: fire is transient, emissive, and lacks consistent correspondences, violating the persistent-primitive/smooth-motion assumptions of current dynamic GS approaches. The analysis of three recurring failure modes (geometric absorption, depth collapse, temporal drift) is well-motivated and supported by experiments.

The technical formulation is sensible and well-integrated: decoupling static background (3DGS with stereo + monocular depth fusion) from transient flame Gaussians initialized from a fused 3D flow field (Tikhonov-regularized least-squares fusion of per-view optical flow, solved via SVD), with per-Gaussian lifetime and linear velocity. The design choices are justified and ablated.

Significant resource contribution: a new real-world fire dataset (17 scenes, diverse fuels, 400 Hz, three GoPros) captured with a custom, low-cost LED-based sub-frame synchronization scheme exploiting rolling shutter, plus a synthetic Mantaflow/Blender benchmark with ground-truth velocity fields. Code and data release is promised.

The proposed density-weighted volumetric evaluation (DVE) protocol addresses a real gap: standard 2D image metrics are insufficient for dynamic/transient 3D phenomena. The Gauss-Hermite quadrature for computing expected ground-truth velocities under the Gaussian distribution is a reasonable density-aware solution.

Evaluation is relatively comprehensive: masked flame metrics, depth plausibility, video-level CGVQM, velocity-field metrics on synthetic data, per-scene results, and ablations over synchronization, flow initialization, alpha loss, and joint vs. decoupled optimization. Limitations are honestly and substantively discussed.

Reproducibility support is strong: detailed implementation specifics (learning rates, iterations, activations, baseline setups including the unofficial FreeTimeGS implementation and its RoMa initialization issues), compute budget, and hardware details in the supplementary.
weaknesses: The depth-plausibility metric (RMSEdepth) compares rendered depth against a monocular depth prediction from Depth Anything V2 — the same model whose aligned depths the authors' own pipeline uses for regularization. This introduces circularity that likely biases the metric in favor of the proposed method, and its absolute meaningfulness as ground truth for flames is questionable.

Several ablation margins are very small, weakening the claimed importance of some components: the NoSync ablation differs by only ~0.04 dB PSNR and ~0.003 LPIPS on real scenes (despite the elaborate custom synchronization hardware being presented as a key contribution), and RandFlow (random flow initialization) is only marginally worse in visual metrics. The synchronization system appears over-engineered relative to its demonstrated impact, although the synthetic DVE results do show more meaningful differences.

The quantitative comparison is restricted to GS-based baselines, with hyperparameters borrowed from the DyNeRF 'flame salmon' scene. While the authors justify excluding tomographic/physics-informed methods on computational grounds, this choice is somewhat circular, and baseline tuning is not optimized for the fire domain, making the 'all baselines fail' claim harder to calibrate.

The velocity-based DVE evaluation is performed only on three synthetic scenes, and real-world motion accuracy is assessed only qualitatively (stream plots, videos). Since physical plausibility of motion is a central claim, quantitative motion evaluation on real captures (or at least more synthetic scenes) would strengthen the case.

The evaluation protocol holds out every 8th frame from the same training viewpoints for quantitative metrics, so the headline numbers measure interpolation rather than true novel-view synthesis; generalization to new views is only shown qualitatively via trajectories in supplementary videos.

The constant-velocity, Gaussian-lifetime model is a simplification of turbulent flame dynamics (acknowledged by the authors), and the static/dynamic decomposition assumes minimal background-foreground interaction; the impact on smoke-rich or large-scale scenes is not empirically characterized beyond the stated limitation.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored and well-motivated problem: sparse-view (3-camera) reconstruction of transient, emissive fire, where the paper convincingly argues that persistent-primitive/smooth-motion assumptions of existing dynamic GS methods fail (three identified failure modes: geometric absorption, depth collapse, temporal drift).

The transient Gaussian formulation (lifetime + linear velocity + temporal opacity modifier), initialized from a fused 3D flow field obtained via a principled SVD-based projection-constraint solve with Tikhonov regularization, is a sensible and clearly described representational change tailored to fire.

Practical systems contribution: a low-cost ESP32/LED synchronization rig exploiting rolling shutter for ~15 µs sub-frame alignment with commodity GoPro cameras is a useful, reproducible capture solution.

New real-world dataset (17 diverse fire scenes, multiple fuels, 400 Hz, three views) plus synthetic Mantaflow scenes with ground-truth velocity fields; the authors commit to releasing code and data, which supports reproducibility.

Honest and reasonably thorough ablation study, including ablations that reveal trade-offs (e.g., NoMask improves visual metrics but degrades motion accuracy), and a novel density-weighted volumetric evaluation (DVE) protocol that goes beyond frame-wise appearance metrics.
Clear writing, good pipeline description, and an explicit limitations section that accurately identifies the linear-velocity, optical-flow, and static/dynamic-separation assumptions.
weaknesses: Depth evaluation on real data is weak: RMSEdepth is computed against a monocular depth prediction (Depth Anything) after linear alignment rather than any ground-truth geometry, so 'depth plausibility' is measured against the very same class of prior used to regularize the method — this partially circularizes the depth claim.

The synchronization contribution is undercut by the authors' own ablation: NoSync differs by only ~0.04 dB PSNR (26.89 vs 26.93) and nearly identical DVE, suggesting the elaborate sub-frame sync hardware provides negligible measured benefit in the reported experiments.

Real-world validation frames are held out every 8th frame, i.e., temporally interleaved between training frames at 400 Hz; this tests interpolation, not temporal generalization, and there is no ground-truth 3D or velocity evidence on real captures — physical plausibility rests entirely on 3 synthetic scenes.

The DVE protocol is evaluated on only 3 synthetic scenes (150 velocity fields from 3 simulations), which is a thin basis for a headline novel metric; its sensitivity and correlation with human perception of motion quality are not validated.

Comparison is restricted to four GS baselines; the exclusion of tomographic/physics-informed volumetric methods is justified by cost, but at least one such comparison (even at reduced settings) would strengthen the claim that no existing approach can reconstruct fire under sparse views.

Several methodological details are heuristic and under-justified: lifetime fixed at 4x frame time, depth loss scaled by 100, alpha loss weight 0.1, disabling densification pruning for the static scene, artificially clamped dynamic Gaussian scales — robustness to these choices is not analyzed.

Fixed three-camera rig with static background assumption limits applicability; smoke-rich scenes (an acknowledged limitation) are barely represented in the dataset, despite smoke being common in real fire.

The velocity model (constant linear velocity) is a strong simplification for turbulent flames; quantitative evidence that the reconstructed velocity field is physically meaningful is limited to coarse L2/CosSim aggregates and one X-slice visualization.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly articulated problem: the paper convincingly identifies why persistent-primitive, smooth-motion assumptions of existing dynamic GS methods fail for transient, emissive phenomena like fire, and analyzes concrete failure modes (geometric absorption, depth collapse, temporal drift).

Sensible and coherent technical design: separating static/dynamic reconstruction, flow-based 3D initialization via a well-derived SVD fusion of multi-view optical flow with Tikhonov regularization, and transient Gaussians with lifetime/velocity directly initialized from the flow field are well-aligned with the problem structure.

Practical systems contribution: the ESP32-based LED synchronization exploiting rolling shutter to achieve ~15 µs sub-frame alignment with consumer GoPro cameras is a genuinely useful, reusable engineering contribution for high-speed multi-view capture.

New evaluation protocol (DVE) addressing a real gap: density-weighted volumetric velocity comparison against simulation ground truth via Gauss-Hermite quadrature is a thoughtful metric for transient phenomena where PSNR/SSIM are insufficient, complemented by the CGVQM video metric.

Comprehensive experiments: 17 real fire scenes across diverse fuels/backgrounds, 3 synthetic Mantaflow scenes with ground-truth velocity fields, comparisons against four strong dynamic GS baselines, per-scene results, video metrics, and thorough ablations (sync, flow init, alpha loss, joint optimization) with an honest discussion of the visual-vs-physical fidelity trade-off (NoMask).

Reproducibility: dataset and code release promised, implementation details (learning rates, iterations, hardware, baseline configurations) are given in the supplementary, and limitations are discussed candidly.
weaknesses: Novelty of the representation itself is limited: the constant-velocity, lifetime-parameterized dynamic Gaussian is adopted from FreeTimeGS [89]; the contribution lies mainly in initialization, decomposition, and capture, which the authors acknowledge, but reviewers should weigh that the core primitive is not new.

Circularity concern in depth evaluation: RMSE_depth compares rendered depth against monocular depth (Depth Anything V2), which is also used as a training regularizer for the static scene and indirectly shapes the reconstruction. This partially favors the proposed method over baselines that did not optimize against this prior; an independent depth reference (e.g., from a denser camera or the synthetic scenes) would strengthen the claim.

Quantitative evaluation on real data uses held-out frames from the same training cameras; no quantitative novel-view evaluation is reported (novel trajectories are only shown qualitatively in the supplementary video).

Some ablation deltas are small: NoSync is nearly indistinguishable from the full method on real-world metrics, weakening the practical importance of the synchronization hardware for the reported capture rates; the benefit likely only manifests at higher speeds, which is not directly demonstrated.

The DVE protocol is evaluated on only 3 synthetic scenes, and as a newly proposed metric it lacks validation against human judgment or established alternatives; the reported '150 synthetic velocity fields' is also unclear relative to 3 scenes.

Comparison is restricted to GS baselines with the efficiency argument; this is reasonable but leaves the accuracy frontier (e.g., tomographic or physics-informed methods) untested, and hyperparameters borrowed from the DyNeRF flame_salmon scene may not be optimal for the baselines.

NoMask ablation outperforms the full method on most real-world visual metrics, indicating the alpha loss trades visual quality for motion plausibility; the paper discusses this but the practical default choice could be better justified.
